However, I have a number of suggestions to enable future cohorts to better get the most out of it: 1) Limit the quotas for a certain number of students (19 is too big of a class size to ensure proper in-depth discussion and effective learning in this course). This would also mean opening more courses within the department to ensure that POLS/non-POLS  students are not taking this course simply because they had no other electives to choose from. 2) If the class size fluctuates and increases independently of the instructor's preferences, assignments need to be tailored accordingly. A suggestion could be to make a certain number of response papers, say 4-5, compulsory to avoid overloading the instructor. Alternatively, or in parallel, the final essay could replace the final exam and be given more importance in the overall assessment weightage of the course. 3) AI proved to be a recurrent challenge that the instructor warned the students about repeatedly. In the future, and perhaps with the TA's help, more systematic screening could take place at the earlier stages of the course and appropriate sanctions be taken. 4) The spare hour is a good way to catch up if we spent too much time in a given week on a concept. Again, communicating early on that a spare hour will be used in the week can help more students stay in class for an extra hour. Overall, Nedim hoca's strength - his kindness towards students - was also a weakness when it came to managing diverging opinions in a bigger classroom. More firmness in the instructor's decision-making regarding the course assessment and conduct of the class, with perhaps leaving less space for spontaneous comments, would be welcome in future recensions of the course.
